claim: Extrahepatic tissues which oxidise ketone bodies also have the capacity to accumulate them under particular conditions.
source: Extrahepatic tissues which oxidise ketone bodies also have the capacity to accumulate them under particular conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general principle underlying the study hypothesis.

claim: β-hydroxybutyrate accumulated in the ischaemic heart to 23.9 nmol/gww.
source: Combining a Langendorff heart model of low-flow ischaemia/reperfusion with liquid chromatography coupled tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS), we show that β-hydroxybutyrate (β-OHB) accumulated in the ischaemic heart to 23.9 nmol/gww and was secreted into the coronary effluent.
evidence: This is a direct measurement reported from LC-MS/MS analysis of ischaemic heart tissue.

claim: β-hydroxybutyrate was secreted into the coronary effluent during ischaemia.
source: Combining a Langendorff heart model of low-flow ischaemia/reperfusion with liquid chromatography coupled tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS), we show that β-hydroxybutyrate (β-OHB) accumulated in the ischaemic heart to 23.9 nmol/gww and was secreted into the coronary effluent.
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data from coronary effluent measurements.

claim: Sodium oxamate increased ischaemic β-OHB levels 5.3-fold.
source: Sodium oxamate, a lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) inhibitor, increased ischaemic β-OHB levels 5.3-fold and slowed contractile recovery.
evidence: This is a measured effect of sodium oxamate treatment on β-OHB levels.

claim: Sodium oxamate slowed contractile recovery.
source: Sodium oxamate, a lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) inhibitor, increased ischaemic β-OHB levels 5.3-fold and slowed contractile recovery.
evidence: This is an observed functional outcome from the experimental intervention.

claim: Inhibition of HMGCS2 with hymeglusin lowered ischaemic β-OHB accumulation by 40%.
source: Inhibition of β-hydroxy-β-methylglutaryl (HMG)-CoA synthase (HMGCS2) with hymeglusin lowered ischaemic β-OHB accumulation by 40%, despite increased flux through succinyl-CoA-3-oxaloacid CoA transferase (SCOT), resulting in greater contractile recovery.
evidence: This is a measured effect of hymeglusin treatment on β-OHB levels.

claim: Hymeglusin treatment increased flux through SCOT despite lowering β-OHB accumulation.
source: Inhibition of β-hydroxy-β-methylglutaryl (HMG)-CoA synthase (HMGCS2) with hymeglusin lowered ischaemic β-OHB accumulation by 40%, despite increased flux through succinyl-CoA-3-oxaloacid CoA transferase (SCOT), resulting in greater contractile recovery.
evidence: This is inferred from metabolite measurements showing changes in succinate and succinyl-CoA levels.

claim: Hymeglusin treatment resulted in greater contractile recovery from ischaemia/reperfusion.
source: Inhibition of β-hydroxy-β-methylglutaryl (HMG)-CoA synthase (HMGCS2) with hymeglusin lowered ischaemic β-OHB accumulation by 40%, despite increased flux through succinyl-CoA-3-oxaloacid CoA transferase (SCOT), resulting in greater contractile recovery.
evidence: This is a measured functional outcome from the experimental intervention.

claim: Hymeglusin protected cardiac mitochondrial respiratory capacity during ischaemia/reperfusion.
source: Hymeglusin also protected cardiac mitochondrial respiratory capacity during ischaemia/reperfusion.
evidence: This is measured through high-resolution respirometry experiments.

claim: Net ketone generation occurs in the heart under conditions of low-flow ischaemia.
source: In conclusion, net ketone generation occurs in the heart under conditions of low-flow ischaemia.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing β-OHB accumulation and secretion.

claim: Ketone generation in the ischaemic heart is driven by flux through both HMGCS2 and SCOT.
source: The process is driven by flux through both HMGCS2 and SCOT, and impacts on cardiac functional recovery from ischaemia/reperfusion.
evidence: This is inferred from the effects of HMGCS2 inhibition and metabolite measurements.

claim: Ketone generation impacts on cardiac functional recovery from ischaemia/reperfusion.
source: The process is driven by flux through both HMGCS2 and SCOT, and impacts on cardiac functional recovery from ischaemia/reperfusion.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the functional recovery differences observed with hymeglusin treatment.

claim: Hepatic ketogenesis plays a vital role in starvation physiology.
source: Hepatic ketogenesis plays a vital role in starvation physiology, whereby acetyl-coenzyme A (acetyl-CoA) derived from fatty acid oxidation (FAO) undergoes a stepwise conversion to acetoacetate (AcAc) and β-hydroxybutyrate (β-OHB), which in turn act as fuels for the brain and other extrahepatic tissues (Puchalska and Crawford, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Puchalska and Crawford, 2017.

claim: Acetyl-CoA derived from fatty acid oxidation undergoes stepwise conversion to acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate.
source: Hepatic ketogenesis plays a vital role in starvation physiology, whereby acetyl-coenzyme A (acetyl-CoA) derived from fatty acid oxidation (FAO) undergoes a stepwise conversion to acetoacetate (AcAc) and β-hydroxybutyrate (β-OHB), which in turn act as fuels for the brain and other extrahepatic tissues (Puchalska and Crawford, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ketogenesis cited from Puchalska and Crawford, 2017.

claim: Ketone bodies act as fuels for the brain and other extrahepatic tissues.
source: Hepatic ketogenesis plays a vital role in starvation physiology, whereby acetyl-coenzyme A (acetyl-CoA) derived from fatty acid oxidation (FAO) undergoes a stepwise conversion to acetoacetate (AcAc) and β-hydroxybutyrate (β-OHB), which in turn act as fuels for the brain and other extrahepatic tissues (Puchalska and Crawford, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Puchalska and Crawford, 2017.

claim: Mitochondrial thiolase catalyses the formation of acetoacetyl-CoA from two acetyl-CoA monomers.
source: Initially, mitochondrial thiolase activity catalyses the formation of acetoacetyl-CoA (AcAc-CoA) from two acetyl-CoA monomers, before a mitochondrial isoform of β-hydroxy-β-methylglutaryl (HMG)-CoA synthase (HMGCS2) catalyses the condensation of AcAc-CoA and a further acetyl-CoA to form HMG-CoA.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about the ketogenesis pathway.

claim: HMGCS2 catalyses the condensation of acetoacetyl-CoA and acetyl-CoA to form HMG-CoA.
source: Initially, mitochondrial thiolase activity catalyses the formation of acetoacetyl-CoA (AcAc-CoA) from two acetyl-CoA monomers, before a mitochondrial isoform of β-hydroxy-β-methylglutaryl (HMG)-CoA synthase (HMGCS2) catalyses the condensation of AcAc-CoA and a further acetyl-CoA to form HMG-CoA.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about the ketogenesis pathway.

claim: The HMGCS2 reaction is considered the rate-limiting step of ketogenesis.
source: This latter reaction is considered the rate-limiting step of ketogenesis, with the significant ketogenic capacity of liver attributed to the uniquely high activity of HMG-CoA synthase in comparison with other tissues (McGarry and Foster, 1976).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from McGarry and Foster, 1976.

claim: The significant ketogenic capacity of liver is attributed to the uniquely high activity of HMG-CoA synthase compared to other tissues.
source: This latter reaction is considered the rate-limiting step of ketogenesis, with the significant ketogenic capacity of liver attributed to the uniquely high activity of HMG-CoA synthase in comparison with other tissues (McGarry and Foster, 1976).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from McGarry and Foster, 1976.

claim: HMG-CoA lyase converts HMG-CoA to acetoacetate in the mitochondria.
source: In the mitochondria, HMG-CoA lyase converts HMG-CoA to AcAc, which in turn is reversibly converted to β-OHB under reducing conditions by β-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase (BDH1).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about the ketogenesis pathway.

claim: Acetoacetate is reversibly converted to β-OHB under reducing conditions by BDH1.
source: In the mitochondria, HMG-CoA lyase converts HMG-CoA to AcAc, which in turn is reversibly converted to β-OHB under reducing conditions by β-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase (BDH1).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about the ketogenesis pathway.

claim: In extrahepatic tissues, BDH1 catalyses the reverse reaction converting β-OHB to acetoacetate.
source: In extrahepatic tissues (Figure 1), BDH1 catalyses the reverse reaction converting β-OHB to AcAc, from which AcAc-CoA is obtained by the exchange of a CoA through the action of succinyl-CoA:3-oxaloacid CoA transferase (SCOT).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about ketone body oxidation in extrahepatic tissues, illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: SCOT obtains acetoacetyl-CoA from acetoacetate by exchanging a CoA.
source: In extrahepatic tissues (Figure 1), BDH1 catalyses the reverse reaction converting β-OHB to AcAc, from which AcAc-CoA is obtained by the exchange of a CoA through the action of succinyl-CoA:3-oxaloacid CoA transferase (SCOT).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about ketone body oxidation, illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Mitochondrial thiolase yields two acetyl-CoA molecules from acetoacetyl-CoA.
source: Mitochondrial thiolase activity then yields two acetyl-CoA molecules, which enter the Krebs cycle.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about ketone body oxidation.

claim: The heart has a significant capacity for ketone body oxidation.
source: The heart has a significant capacity for ketone body oxidation (Cotter et al., 2013), but any extrahepatic tissue which oxidises ketone bodies also has the capacity to generate ketone bodies (Puchalska and Crawford, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Cotter et al., 2013.

claim: Any extrahepatic tissue which oxidises ketone bodies also has the capacity to generate ketone bodies.
source: The heart has a significant capacity for ketone body oxidation (Cotter et al., 2013), but any extrahepatic tissue which oxidises ketone bodies also has the capacity to generate ketone bodies (Puchalska and Crawford, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Puchalska and Crawford, 2017.

claim: Ketone body generation occurs in the kidney through the reversible enzymatic activity of mitochondrial thiolase and SCOT.
source: This was shown to occur in the kidney through the reversible enzymatic activity of mitochondrial thiolase and SCOT, and the authors speculated that this may generally be the case for extrahepatic tissues (Weidemann and Krebs, 1969).
evidence: This is cited from Weidemann and Krebs, 1969.

claim: Net production of acetoacetate and β-OHB has been observed in the isolated perfused rat heart when fatty acids are supplied via the perfusion medium.
source: In the isolated perfused rat heart, net production of AcAc and β-OHB has been observed when fatty acids are supplied via the perfusion medium (Comte et al., 1997; Opie and Owen, 1975).
evidence: This is cited from Comte et al., 1997 and Opie and Owen, 1975.

claim: Fatty acid oxidation is implicated as a source of ketone body efflux in the perfused heart.
source: Inclusion of [1-13C]octanoate in the medium and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) analysis of ketone body enrichments in the coronary effluent implicated FAO as a source of this ketone body efflux (Comte et al., 1997), which may represent a spillover pathway when acetyl-CoA availability exceeds the capacity of the Krebs cycle.
evidence: This is cited from Comte et al., 1997 using isotope tracing experiments.

claim: Ketone body production may represent a spillover pathway when acetyl-CoA availability exceeds the capacity of the Krebs cycle.
source: Inclusion of [1-13C]octanoate in the medium and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) analysis of ketone body enrichments in the coronary effluent implicated FAO as a source of this ketone body efflux (Comte et al., 1997), which may represent a spillover pathway when acetyl-CoA availability exceeds the capacity of the Krebs cycle.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the cited findings.

claim: Net production of acetoacetate from acetyl-CoA was seen in pig heart extracts but only in the presence of succinate.
source: Independent of fatty acid provision, net production of AcAc from acetyl-CoA was seen in pig heart extracts but only in the presence of succinate (Stern et al., 1953), whilst AcAc and β-OHB synthesis was seen in isolated rat heart mitochondria respiring with pyruvate and malate (LaNoue et al., 1970).
evidence: This is cited from Stern et al., 1953.

claim: Acetoacetate and β-OHB synthesis was seen in isolated rat heart mitochondria respiring with pyruvate and malate.
source: Independent of fatty acid provision, net production of AcAc from acetyl-CoA was seen in pig heart extracts but only in the presence of succinate (Stern et al., 1953), whilst AcAc and β-OHB synthesis was seen in isolated rat heart mitochondria respiring with pyruvate and malate (LaNoue et al., 1970).
evidence: This is cited from LaNoue et al., 1970.

claim: The conversion of acetoacetate to β-OHB by BDH1 is dependent on NADH availability.
source: The conversion of AcAc to β-OHB by BDH1 is dependent on NADH availability, and accordingly was found to be increased in the isolated perfused rat heart under anoxic conditions (Opie and Owen, 1975).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge and cited from Opie and Owen, 1975.

claim: Conversion of acetoacetate to β-OHB was increased in the isolated perfused rat heart under anoxic conditions.
source: The conversion of AcAc to β-OHB by BDH1 is dependent on NADH availability, and accordingly was found to be increased in the isolated perfused rat heart under anoxic conditions (Opie and Owen, 1975).
evidence: This is cited from Opie and Owen, 1975.

claim: Reduction of acetoacetate was seen in sheep heart homogenates treated with succinate and the mitochondrial complex I inhibitor amytal.
source: Reduction of AcAc was seen in sheep heart homogenates treated with succinate and the mitochondrial complex I inhibitor amytal (Krebs et al., 1961; Kulka et al., 1961), and complete reduction of AcAc to β-OHB was reported in isolated rat heart mitochondria respiring with succinate (Schönfeld et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Krebs et al., 1961 and Kulka et al., 1961.

claim: Complete reduction of acetoacetate to β-OHB was reported in isolated rat heart mitochondria respiring with succinate.
source: Reduction of AcAc was seen in sheep heart homogenates treated with succinate and the mitochondrial complex I inhibitor amytal (Krebs et al., 1961; Kulka et al., 1961), and complete reduction of AcAc to β-OHB was reported in isolated rat heart mitochondria respiring with succinate (Schönfeld et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Schönfeld et al., 2010.

claim: Net cardiac production of β-OHB can occur under ischaemic conditions when availability of NADH and acetyl-CoA would be increased and when succinate accumulates.
source: We therefore hypothesised that net cardiac production of β-OHB can occur under ischaemic conditions, when availability of NADH and acetyl-CoA would be increased and when succinate accumulates (Chouchani et al., 2014; Laplante et al., 1997; Taegtmeyer, 1978; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is the study hypothesis based on cited literature about ischaemic metabolic changes.

claim: Succinate accumulates during ischaemia.
source: We therefore hypothesised that net cardiac production of β-OHB can occur under ischaemic conditions, when availability of NADH and acetyl-CoA would be increased and when succinate accumulates (Chouchani et al., 2014; Laplante et al., 1997; Taegtmeyer, 1978; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple sources.

claim: The concentration of β-OHB in left ventricle after 32 min of aerobic perfusion was 0.2 nmol per mg tissue.
source: The concentration of β-OHB in left ventricle after 32 min of aerobic perfusion was 0.2 nmol per mg tissue, but following 20 min of low-flow ischaemia (0.56 ml.min−1.gww−1), it accumulated to 23.9 nmol per mg tissue (p<0.01) before returning to 0.7 nmol per mg tissue following reperfusion.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from LC-MS analysis.

claim: Following 20 min of low-flow ischaemia, β-OHB accumulated to 23.9 nmol per mg tissue.
source: The concentration of β-OHB in left ventricle after 32 min of aerobic perfusion was 0.2 nmol per mg tissue, but following 20 min of low-flow ischaemia (0.56 ml.min−1.gww−1), it accumulated to 23.9 nmol per mg tissue (p<0.01) before returning to 0.7 nmol per mg tissue following reperfusion.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from LC-MS analysis with statistical significance.

claim: β-OHB returned to 0.7 nmol per mg tissue following reperfusion.
source: The concentration of β-OHB in left ventricle after 32 min of aerobic perfusion was 0.2 nmol per mg tissue, but following 20 min of low-flow ischaemia (0.56 ml.min−1.gww−1), it accumulated to 23.9 nmol per mg tissue (p<0.01) before returning to 0.7 nmol per mg tissue following reperfusion.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from LC-MS analysis.

claim: β-OHB rose in the coronary effluent throughout ischaemia and returned to a lower level following reperfusion.
source: β-OHB was also seen to rise in the coronary effluent throughout ischaemia, returning to a lower level following reperfusion, suggesting that the myocardial β-OHB was oxidised by the heart upon reperfusion.
evidence: This is observed in the coronary effluent measurements.

claim: Myocardial β-OHB was oxidised by the heart upon reperfusion.
source: β-OHB was also seen to rise in the coronary effluent throughout ischaemia, returning to a lower level following reperfusion, suggesting that the myocardial β-OHB was oxidised by the heart upon reperfusion.
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of β-OHB levels in tissue and effluent.

claim: The myocardial accumulation and efflux of β-OHB during ischaemia mirrored that of lactate.
source: The myocardial accumulation and efflux of β-OHB during ischaemia thereby mirrored that of lactate (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is observed by comparing the patterns in Figure 2A-B with Figure 2C-D.

claim: Cardiac contractile function recovered to 100% of its pre-ischaemic level upon reperfusion in the mild ischaemia protocol.
source: In this protocol, cardiac contractile function recovered to 100% of its pre-ischaemic level upon reperfusion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the functional measurements in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Myocardial acetyl-CoA increased 2.6-fold during ischaemia.
source: The ischaemic accumulation of β-OHB was associated with a 2.6-fold increase in myocardial acetyl-CoA during ischaemia (Figure 2E; p<0.05), a 3.6-fold increase in acetoacetyl-CoA (Figure 2F; p<0.0001), and a 3.4-fold increase in HMG-CoA relative to the pre-ischaemic LV (Figure 2G; p<0.01).
evidence: This is a measured change shown in Figure 2E with statistical significance.

claim: Acetoacetyl-CoA increased 3.6-fold during ischaemia.
source: The ischaemic accumulation of β-OHB was associated with a 2.6-fold increase in myocardial acetyl-CoA during ischaemia (Figure 2E; p<0.05), a 3.6-fold increase in acetoacetyl-CoA (Figure 2F; p<0.0001), and a 3.4-fold increase in HMG-CoA relative to the pre-ischaemic LV (Figure 2G; p<0.01).
evidence: This is a measured change shown in Figure 2F with statistical significance.

claim: HMG-CoA increased 3.4-fold during ischaemia relative to the pre-ischaemic left ventricle.
source: The ischaemic accumulation of β-OHB was associated with a 2.6-fold increase in myocardial acetyl-CoA during ischaemia (Figure 2E; p<0.05), a 3.6-fold increase in acetoacetyl-CoA (Figure 2F; p<0.0001), and a 3.4-fold increase in HMG-CoA relative to the pre-ischaemic LV (Figure 2G; p<0.01).
evidence: This is a measured change shown in Figure 2G with statistical significance.

claim: The increase in HMG-CoA suggested that some flux may occur through HMGCS2 in the ischaemic heart.
source: The unexpected finding of increased HMG-CoA suggested that some flux may occur through HMGCS2 in the ischaemic heart, despite its low activity in the heart in comparison with liver (McGarry and Foster, 1976).
evidence: This is inferred from the unexpected accumulation of HMG-CoA during ischaemia.

claim: HMGCS2 has low activity in the heart in comparison with liver.
source: The unexpected finding of increased HMG-CoA suggested that some flux may occur through HMGCS2 in the ischaemic heart, despite its low activity in the heart in comparison with liver (McGarry and Foster, 1976).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from McGarry and Foster, 1976.

claim: Malondialdehyde was 2.3-fold higher in the ischaemic heart compared with the non-ischaemic heart.
source: The lipid peroxidation marker malondialdehyde (MDA) was also 2.3-fold higher in the ischaemic heart compared with the non-ischaemic heart, demonstrating oxidative stress (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; p<0.05).
evidence: This is a measured change shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 with statistical significance.

claim: Elevated malondialdehyde demonstrates oxidative stress in the ischaemic heart.
source: The lipid peroxidation marker malondialdehyde (MDA) was also 2.3-fold higher in the ischaemic heart compared with the non-ischaemic heart, demonstrating oxidative stress (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; p<0.05).
evidence: This is inferred from the known role of MDA as a lipid peroxidation marker.

claim: Succinate increased 4.3-fold during ischaemia.
source: As expected, 4-carbon intermediates accumulated during ischaemia (Figure 3), including a 4.3-fold increase in succinate (p<0.01), which is known to augment the reduction of acetoacetate to β-OHB (Schönfeld et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a measured change shown in Figure 3 with statistical significance.

claim: Succinate is known to augment the reduction of acetoacetate to β-OHB.
source: As expected, 4-carbon intermediates accumulated during ischaemia (Figure 3), including a 4.3-fold increase in succinate (p<0.01), which is known to augment the reduction of acetoacetate to β-OHB (Schönfeld et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Schönfeld et al., 2010.

claim: Myocardial citrate concentrations during ischaemia were 65% lower than pre-ischaemic levels.
source: Meanwhile, myocardial citrate concentrations during ischaemia were 65% lower than pre-ischaemic levels (p<0.05), which in conjunction with the accumulation of acetyl-CoA (Figure 2E) suggested lower citrate synthase activity during ischaemia.
evidence: This is a measured change with statistical significance.

claim: Lower citrate levels in conjunction with acetyl-CoA accumulation suggested lower citrate synthase activity during ischaemia.
source: Meanwhile, myocardial citrate concentrations during ischaemia were 65% lower than pre-ischaemic levels (p<0.05), which in conjunction with the accumulation of acetyl-CoA (Figure 2E) suggested lower citrate synthase activity during ischaemia.
evidence: This is inferred from the metabolite patterns observed.

claim: Lactate efflux into the coronary effluent was 4.4-fold lower with oxamate treatment compared to non-treated hearts.
source: As expected, when oxamate was present, lactate efflux into the coronary effluent was 4.4-fold lower over the course of the ischaemic period in comparison with non-treated hearts (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a measured effect shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Left ventricular lactate levels were elevated 1.44-fold during ischaemia with oxamate treatment.
source: LV lactate levels were unexpectedly elevated 1.44-fold during ischaemia as a result of oxamate (Figure 4B; p<0.01), perhaps suggesting impaired lactate efflux.
evidence: This is a measured effect shown in Figure 4B with statistical significance.

claim: Elevated left ventricular lactate with oxamate treatment suggests impaired lactate efflux.
source: LV lactate levels were unexpectedly elevated 1.44-fold during ischaemia as a result of oxamate (Figure 4B; p<0.01), perhaps suggesting impaired lactate efflux.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the unexpected finding.

claim: Pyruvate concentrations were 2.5-fold higher with oxamate treatment.
source: In accordance with the expected effects of LDH inhibition, pyruvate and acetyl-CoA concentrations were 2.5- and 1.5-fold higher, respectively, following oxamate treatment (Figure 4C–D; p<0.01 and p<0.05, respectively).
evidence: This is a measured effect shown in Figure 4C with statistical significance.

claim: Acetyl-CoA concentrations were 1.5-fold higher with oxamate treatment.
source: In accordance with the expected effects of LDH inhibition, pyruvate and acetyl-CoA concentrations were 2.5- and 1.5-fold higher, respectively, following oxamate treatment (Figure 4C–D; p<0.01 and p<0.05, respectively).
evidence: This is a measured effect shown in Figure 4D with statistical significance.

claim: Acetoacetyl-CoA levels were 7.2-fold greater with oxamate treatment.
source: The increase in ischaemic acetyl-CoA was reflected in 7.2-fold greater levels of acetoacetyl-CoA and 1.8-fold greater levels of HMG-CoA (Figure 4E–F; p<0.0001 and p<0.05).
evidence: This is a measured effect shown in Figure 4E with statistical significance.

claim: HMG-CoA levels were 1.8-fold greater with oxamate treatment.
source: The increase in ischaemic acetyl-CoA was reflected in 7.2-fold greater levels of acetoacetyl-CoA and 1.8-fold greater levels of HMG-CoA (Figure 4E–F; p<0.0001 and p<0.05).
evidence: This is a measured effect shown in Figure 4F with statistical significance.

claim: Sodium oxamate treatment resulted in 5.3-fold greater β-OHB accumulation during ischaemia.
source: Sodium oxamate treatment also resulted in 5.3-fold greater β-OHB accumulation during ischaemia (Figure 4G; p<0.001).
evidence: This is a measured effect shown in Figure 4G with statistical significance.

claim: Oxamate treatment resulted in 2.7-fold greater initial secretion of β-OHB into the perfusate during ischaemia at 36 min.
source: There was also a 2.7-fold greater initial secretion of β-OHB into the perfusate during ischaemia at 36 min (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; p<0.001), although this secretion decreased as the ischaemic period progressed, reaching 0 at 60 min before again rising to 44-fold higher than pre-ischaemia upon reperfusion (p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a measured effect shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 with statistical significance.

claim: β-OHB secretion with oxamate decreased as the ischaemic period progressed, reaching 0 at 60 min.
source: There was also a 2.7-fold greater initial secretion of β-OHB into the perfusate during ischaemia at 36 min (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; p<0.001), although this secretion decreased as the ischaemic period progressed, reaching 0 at 60 min before again rising to 44-fold higher than pre-ischaemia upon reperfusion (p<0.0001).
evidence: This is observed in the time course data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: β-OHB secretion rose to 44-fold higher than pre-ischaemia upon reperfusion with oxamate treatment.
source: There was also a 2.7-fold greater initial secretion of β-OHB into the perfusate during ischaemia at 36 min (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; p<0.001), although this secretion decreased as the ischaemic period progressed, reaching 0 at 60 min before again rising to 44-fold higher than pre-ischaemia upon reperfusion (p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a measured effect shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 with statistical significance.

claim: Succinyl-CoA was present at 2.2-fold greater levels in oxamate-treated hearts during ischaemia.
source: Furthermore, succinyl-CoA was present at 2.2-fold greater levels in oxamate-treated hearts during ischaemia compared with untreated hearts, whilst succinate levels were 32% lower (Figure 4H–I; p<0.001 and p<0.0001), suggesting that reverse flux through SCOT contributes to the production of β-OHB in the ischaemic heart (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is a measured effect shown in Figure 4H with statistical significance.

claim: Succinate levels were 32% lower in oxamate-treated hearts during ischaemia.
source: Furthermore, succinyl-CoA was present at 2.2-fold greater levels in oxamate-treated hearts during ischaemia compared with untreated hearts, whilst succinate levels were 32% lower (Figure 4H–I; p<0.001 and p<0.0001), suggesting that reverse flux through SCOT contributes to the production of β-OHB in the ischaemic heart (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is a measured effect shown in Figure 4I with statistical significance.

claim: Reverse flux through SCOT contributes to the production of β-OHB in the ischaemic heart.
source: Furthermore, succinyl-CoA was present at 2.2-fold greater levels in oxamate-treated hearts during ischaemia compared with untreated hearts, whilst succinate levels were 32% lower (Figure 4H–I; p<0.001 and p<0.0001), suggesting that reverse flux through SCOT contributes to the production of β-OHB in the ischaemic heart (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of succinyl-CoA and succinate changes with oxamate treatment.

claim: Sodium oxamate administration led to slower recovery of contractile function post-reperfusion.
source: Sodium oxamate administration, and its associated metabolic changes, led to slower recovery of contractile function post-reperfusion in comparison with control hearts (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in the functional recovery data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Ischaemic levels of lipid peroxidation were 51% greater with oxamate treatment than in control hearts.
source: Ischaemic levels of lipid peroxidation were also 51% greater than in control hearts (Figure 4—figure supplement 3; p<0.05).
evidence: This is a measured effect shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3 with statistical significance.

claim: Hymeglusin treatment resulted in 27% lower ischaemic lactate accumulation.
source: Treatment with hymeglusin resulted in 27% lower ischaemic lactate accumulation (Figure 5A; p<0.05), while pyruvate concentrations in ischaemia were unaffected (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a measured effect shown in Figure 5A with statistical significance.

claim: Pyruvate concentrations in ischaemia were unaffected by hymeglusin treatment.
source: Treatment with hymeglusin resulted in 27% lower ischaemic lactate accumulation (Figure 5A; p<0.05), while pyruvate concentrations in ischaemia were unaffected (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B where no significant difference is observed.

claim: Acetyl-CoA levels were 5.1-fold greater in hearts where HMGCS2 was inhibited.
source: Meanwhile, acetyl-CoA levels were 5.1-fold greater (Figure 5C; p<0.01) in hearts where HMGCS2 was inhibited.
evidence: This is a measured effect shown in Figure 5C with statistical significance.

claim: Hymeglusin administration led to a 7.6-fold ischaemic accumulation of acetoacetyl-CoA.
source: Hymeglusin administration led to a 7.6-fold ischaemic accumulation of acetoacetyl-CoA (a substrate for HMGCS2), and a 65% lower level of HMG-CoA (Figure 5D–E; both p<0.01), suggesting that inhibition of HMGCS2 was effective.
evidence: This is a measured effect shown in Figure 5D with statistical significance.

claim: Hymeglusin administration resulted in a 65% lower level of HMG-CoA.
source: Hymeglusin administration led to a 7.6-fold ischaemic accumulation of acetoacetyl-CoA (a substrate for HMGCS2), and a 65% lower level of HMG-CoA (Figure 5D–E; both p<0.01), suggesting that inhibition of HMGCS2 was effective.
evidence: This is a measured effect shown in Figure 5E with statistical significance.

claim: The accumulation of acetoacetyl-CoA and depletion of HMG-CoA with hymeglusin suggests that inhibition of HMGCS2 was effective.

claim: Hymeglusin resulted in a 40% lower ischaemic accumulation of β-OHB in the left ventricle compared with vehicle-treated hearts.

evidence: This is a measured effect shown in Figure 5F with statistical significance.

claim: Hymeglusin resulted in a 41% lower level of succinate in ischaemic hearts.

evidence: This is a measured effect shown in Figure 5G with statistical significance.

claim: Hymeglusin resulted in a 2.7-fold greater level of succinyl-CoA in ischaemic hearts.

claim: Hymeglusin administration resulted in 33% greater recovery of cardiac contractile function upon reperfusion.
source: Hymeglusin administration 12 min before ischaemia resulted in 33% greater recovery of cardiac contractile function upon reperfusion, relative to untreated controls (Figure 6A).

claim: At 52, 56, and 60 min during the ischaemic period, 40, 43, and 35% lower levels of β-OHB were detected in the coronary effluent from hymeglusin-administered hearts.
source: At 52, 56, and 60 min during the ischaemic period, 40, 43, and 35% lower levels of β-OHB were detected in the coronary effluent from hymeglusin-administered hearts relative to control hearts (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; p<0.01, p<0.05, and p<0.05, respectively).
evidence: This is shown in the coronary effluent measurements in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 with statistical significance.

claim: Ischaemia/reperfusion resulted in 36% lower β-oxidation-supported OXPHOS capacity relative to control hearts.
source: Moreover, ischaemia/reperfusion (I/R) resulted in impaired mitochondrial respiratory capacities relative to control hearts perfused for 96 min without ischaemia (Figure 6B), with 36% lower β-oxidation-supported oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) capacity (p<0.001), 36% lower β-oxidation + pyruvate-supported OXPHOS capacity (p<0.05), 31% lower complex I capacity (p<0.05), and a 42% impairment of respiratory capacity supported by complex I and II (p<0.001).
evidence: This is measured through high-resolution respirometry shown in Figure 6B with statistical significance.

claim: Ischaemia/reperfusion resulted in 36% lower β-oxidation + pyruvate-supported OXPHOS capacity.

claim: Administration of hymeglusin prior to ischaemia/reperfusion attenuated the post-ischaemic impairment of cardiac mitochondrial respiratory capacity.

claim: There was no significant difference between respiratory capacity of hymeglusin-treated ischaemia/reperfusion hearts and time-matched non-ischaemic controls.

claim: Complex II capacity was not significantly affected by ischaemia.

claim: Hymeglusin resulted in a post-reperfusion complex II capacity which was 74% greater than in the vehicle-treated heart.
source: Complex II capacity was not significantly affected by ischaemia; however, hymeglusin resulted in a post-reperfusion complex II capacity which was 74% greater than in the vehicle-treated heart (p<0.05) and not significantly different to non-ischaemic time-matched controls.
evidence: This is measured through high-resolution respirometry with statistical significance.

claim: Hymeglusin administration resulted in 38% lower ischaemic levels of malondialdehyde.
source: Hymeglusin administration also resulted in 38% lower ischaemic levels of the lipid peroxidation marker malondialdehyde (Figure 6—figure supplement 2; p<0.05).

claim: Most myocardial β-OHB appeared to result from reverse flux through SCOT.
source: Whilst most myocardial β-OHB appeared to result from reverse flux through SCOT, we unexpectedly found that at least some β-OHB production occurred via the production of HMG-CoA by HMGCS2.
evidence: This is inferred from the metabolite patterns and effects of HMGCS2 inhibition.

claim: At least some β-OHB production occurred via the production of HMG-CoA by HMGCS2.
source: Whilst most myocardial β-OHB appeared to result from reverse flux through SCOT, we unexpectedly found that at least some β-OHB production occurred via the production of HMG-CoA by HMGCS2.

claim: Inhibition of HMGCS2 lowered myocardial levels of HMG-CoA and suppressed β-OHB in the ischaemic heart despite an apparent increase in reverse flux through SCOT.
source: Indeed, inhibition of HMGCS2 lowered myocardial levels of HMG-CoA and suppressed β-OHB in the ischaemic heart despite an apparent increase in reverse flux through SCOT.

claim: HMGCS2 inhibition was associated with enhanced functional recovery from ischaemia/reperfusion.

claim: HMGCS2 inhibition was associated with protection of mitochondrial respiratory function in the post-ischaemic rat heart.
source: This was associated with enhanced functional recovery from ischaemia/reperfusion and protection of mitochondrial respiratory function in the post-ischaemic rat heart.

claim: The combination of mass spectrometry and Langendorff perfusion allowed tight control of metabolic substrate supply to the heart.
source: Our approach exploited the combination of mass spectrometry and Langendorff perfusion, which allowed a tight control of metabolic substrate supply to the heart, which is unattainable in vivo.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the experimental approach.

claim: Tight control of metabolic substrate supply is unattainable in vivo.
source: Our approach exploited the combination of mass spectrometry and Langendorff perfusion, which allowed a tight control of metabolic substrate supply to the heart, which is unattainable in vivo.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of in vivo studies compared to ex vivo perfusion.

claim: Mass spectrometry allowed detection of β-OHB and neighbouring metabolites under aerobically perfused and ischaemic conditions.
source: Mass spectrometry allowed us to detect β-OHB and neighbouring metabolites, under aerobically perfused and ischaemic conditions.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the capabilities of the analytical technique used.

claim: Use of the LDH inhibitor sodium oxamate allowed investigation of the implications of enhanced glucose-derived acetyl-CoA upon candidate pathways.
source: Use of the LDH inhibitor sodium oxamate allowed us to investigate the implications of enhanced glucose-derived acetyl-CoA upon candidate pathways.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the experimental strategy.

claim: Impaired functional recovery from ischaemia/reperfusion with LDH inhibition is likely to be more substantially influenced by impaired lactate production than by changes in β-OHB or associated metabolites.
source: We do, however, urge caution when interpreting some of the results of our experiments with LDH inhibition, particularly regarding the functional recovery from I/R, since this is likely to be more substantially influenced by impaired lactate production than by changes in β-OHB or associated metabolites (Griffin et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a cautionary interpretation citing Griffin et al., 2000.

claim: The high concentration of sodium oxamate used is in line with that used by others previously.
source: Moreover, despite the high concentration of sodium oxamate used here being in line with that used by others previously (Yoshioka et al., 2012), it is such that we cannot exclude osmotic effects.
evidence: This is a methodological justification citing Yoshioka et al., 2012.

claim: Osmotic effects cannot be excluded with the high concentration of sodium oxamate used.
source: Moreover, despite the high concentration of sodium oxamate used here being in line with that used by others previously (Yoshioka et al., 2012), it is such that we cannot exclude osmotic effects.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: The use of hymeglusin allowed probing of the unexpected finding that flux through HMGCS2 during ischaemia supports the production of HMG-CoA and β-OHB.
source: The use of hymeglusin allowed us to probe the unexpected finding that flux through HMGCS2 during ischaemia supports the production of HMG-CoA and consequently of β-OHB.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the experimental strategy.

claim: Off-target effects of hymeglusin cannot be definitively excluded.

evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Data showing accumulation of acetoacetyl-CoA coupled with depletion of HMG-CoA indicates that the HMGCS2 pathway was inhibited by hymeglusin.

evidence: This is inferred from the metabolite patterns observed with hymeglusin treatment.

claim: Hymeglusin treatment appeared to increase the reverse flux through SCOT during ischaemia.
source: Hymeglusin treatment itself appeared to increase the reverse flux through SCOT during ischaemia, as evidenced by decreased succinate and increased succinyl-CoA levels relative to untreated hearts.
evidence: This is inferred from the metabolite patterns observed with hymeglusin treatment.

claim: Both SCOT- and HMGCS2-supported pathways contribute to the ischaemic accumulation of β-OHB.
source: Whilst our results therefore suggest that both SCOT- and HMGCS2-supported pathways contribute to the ischaemic accumulation of β-OHB, they do not indicate the relative contributions of each, and flux through SCOT may be the more significant route.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results with both oxamate and hymeglusin.

claim: The relative contributions of SCOT and HMGCS2 pathways to β-OHB accumulation are not indicated by the results.
source: Whilst our results therefore suggest that both SCOT- and HMGCS2-supported pathways contribute to the ischaemic accumulation of β-OHB, they do not indicate the relative contributions of each, and flux through SCOT may be the more significant route.

claim: Flux through SCOT may be the more significant route for β-OHB production.
source: Whilst our results therefore suggest that both SCOT- and HMGCS2-supported pathways contribute to the ischaemic accumulation of β-OHB, they do not indicate the relative contributions of each, and flux through SCOT may be the more significant route.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the results.

claim: The findings add to those of others who have previously reported ketone body production by the ex vivo perfused heart.
source: Our findings add to those of others who have previously reported ketone body production by the ex vivo perfused heart (Comte et al., 1997; Opie and Owen, 1975), in myocardial extracts (Stern et al., 1953) and in isolated cardiac mitochondria (LaNoue et al., 1970), and support the notion that ketone body production may represent a spillover pathway for excess acetyl-CoA.
evidence: This contextualizes the findings within existing literature.

claim: Myocardial ketone body production may occur under hypoxic/ischaemic conditions in vivo.
source: Whilst it has not been conclusively demonstrated, a number of studies have suggested that myocardial ketone body production may also occur under hypoxic/ischaemic conditions in vivo.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature.

source: In studies of dogs, hypoxaemia resulted in enhanced β-OHB:acetoacetate and net myocardial acetoacetate production in some animals, whilst this was not seen in any non-hypoxaemic dogs (Whereat and Chan, 1972).

claim: Animals exhibiting net acetoacetate production had arterial lactate concentrations in excess of 5 mM, suggesting a high degree of hypoxic stress.
source: Notably, those animals exhibiting net acetoacetate production had arterial lactate concentrations in excess of 5 mM, suggesting a high degree of hypoxic stress (Whereat and Chan, 1972).

claim: Serum levels of β-OHB and acetoacetate increased systemically in human patients following balloon-induced coronary ischaemia during elective coronary angioplasty.

evidence: This is cited from Di Marino et al., 2018.

claim: Myocardial β-OHB utilisation was suppressed during myocardial ischaemia in patients experiencing angina-like chest pain.

claim: Efflux of β-OHB is seen shortly after the onset of ischaemia.
source: Efflux of β-OHB is seen shortly after the onset of ischaemia, and its production is therefore likely to result from altered substrate availability and/or post-translational modifications rather than altered gene expression.

claim: β-OHB production during ischaemia is likely to result from altered substrate availability and/or post-translational modifications rather than altered gene expression.

claim: Mitochondrial reactive oxygen species are produced during ischaemia.

claim: Acetyl-CoA, succinate, and ROS may post-translationally modify proteins and thereby support ketone flux.

evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed by the authors.

claim: HMGCS2 is expressed in human heart, albeit at a lower level than in liver.
source: HMGCS2 is expressed in human heart, albeit at a lower level than in liver (Mascaró et al., 1995), and whilst activity levels of HMGCS2 and HMG-CoA lyase are, respectively, 20-fold and 6.8-fold higher in adult rat liver than heart, activity in the myocardium exceeds that in brain or skeletal muscle (McGarry and Foster, 1976).
evidence: This is cited from Mascaró et al., 1995.

claim: Activity levels of HMGCS2 are 20-fold higher in adult rat liver than heart.

claim: The role of cardiac HMGCS2 is unknown.
source: Although the role of cardiac HMGCS2 is unknown, it is transiently expressed at a high level in neonatal mouse heart before declining by postnatal day 23 (Talman et al., 2018) and has been shown to be upregulated in type 1 diabetes following streptozotocin (STZ) treatment in rats (Cook et al., 2017) and mice (Shukla et al., 2017), as well as in mice when fasted or on a ketogenic diet (Wentz et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Heart-specific overexpression of HMGCS2 resulted in increased cardiac β-OHB, along with mitochondrial swelling and systolic impairment.

claim: Inhibition of HMGCS2 was associated with protection of mitochondrial respiratory capacity in the post-ischaemic rat heart and enhanced functional recovery from ischaemia/reperfusion.

claim: The protection from HMGCS2 inhibition is unlikely to arise as a direct result of decreased β-OHB availability.
source: This protection is unlikely to arise as a direct result of decreased β-OHB availability; ketone body administration has been shown to be neuroprotective during ischaemic stroke injury (Yin et al., 2015) and during renal ischaemia/reperfusion (Tajima et al., 2019).
evidence: This is inferred from cited literature showing protective effects of ketone bodies.

claim: Ketone body administration has been shown to be neuroprotective during ischaemic stroke injury.

source: Inhibition of HMGCS2 may therefore represent a novel cardioprotective strategy, perhaps of particular relevance to the diabetic heart, where sensitivity to ischaemia/reperfusion injury (Paulson, 1997) and, at least in the case of type 1 diabetes, expression of HMGCS2 are both increased (Cook et al., 2017; Shukla et al., 2017).
